evidence.label: Graph Decompositions at the Integral Expectation Threshold
Integral and fractional expectation thresholds are equivalent

headline: Spreading credit fractionally beats whole-set covers by at most a fixed factor in Talagrand's threshold theory.
scope: The comparison and discrete-convexity results cover every finite family of sets, with very large fixed constants. The graph decomposition holds piece by piece; the pieces' copies need not line up.
plain: Expectation thresholds give cheap lower estimates for when a random set first has a property. Talagrand asked whether allowing fractional covers changes them by more than a fixed factor. One paper proves it does not, and a second proves his discrete-convexity conjecture. A third paper uses these to claim a graph-decomposition conjecture about random graphs.
doesNot: This does not give constants of practical size, and the graph pieces need not fit together on shared points.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Michel Talagrand, who posed both conjectures
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles two of Talagrand's conjectures on thresholds and applies them to a recent graph conjecture.

explanation:
Take ten lights. Each one turns on by itself with chance p, independently. Ask when at least five are on with probability one half. An exact count of the cases gives p of about 0.452. That number is the threshold for the event "at least five on".

There is a cheaper estimate, built from covers. Any five lights that are on form one of 252 possible groups. Each group is fully on with chance p⁵. Add these up: 252p⁵. While that sum is at most one half, the event cannot happen half the time. The sum reaches one half at p of about 0.288. So 0.288 is a safe lower estimate. Such a list of small sets, one inside every outcome of the event, is an integral cover. The best p a cover can certify, with total cost at most one half, is the integral expectation threshold.

Talagrand also allowed fractional covers. Instead of picking whole sets, you spread credit. Each outcome of the event must collect total credit of at least 1 from the sets inside it. Put credit 1/5 on each single light. Any five lights then collect exactly 1. The cost is 10 × 1/5 × p, which is 2p. That works up to p of 0.25, so this particular fractional cover does worse. In general, fractional covers have more freedom. So the fractional threshold is at least the integral one[1].

Michel Talagrand conjectured around 2010 that the extra freedom gains at most a fixed factor[2]. This mattered because of a related result. Park and Pham proved the Kahn–Kalai conjecture with integral covers[3]. Earlier work had compared fractional and integral covers only in special cases. Talagrand handled covers made of single elements[4]. Later work reached a loss of order log log of the number of elements[5]. Park then removed that dependence, but his factor still grew as the threshold got small[6].

One paper proves Talagrand's conjecture, removing both kinds of growth[7]. The fractional threshold is at most 25 × 512⁴ times the integral one. That is about 1.7 trillion. The number is huge, but it is the same for every family of sets, however large[8].

A second paper proves a related conjecture of Talagrand, about discrete convexity[9]. Take a family of sets that a random set lands in very often. Talagrand predicted that unions of a fixed number of its members contain almost everything[10]. The sets left over should have a cheap integral cover. The paper proves this with the fixed number 2⁷⁵, for any family at all[11].

A third paper applies these ideas to random graphs. It claims the graph-decomposition conjecture of Ascoli, He, Park and Talagrand[12]. Any target graph splits into a fixed number of pieces. Each piece appears in a random graph at a density within a fixed factor of the integral threshold[13]. Without splitting, the known bound loses a logarithmic factor[14]. There is a catch. Each piece appears somewhere, but the copies need not fit together on shared points[15]. That proof uses the discrete-convexity theorem as its main input[16]. The hard part was the links between points with many neighbors and points with few[17]. Knowing that a class of graphs is typical was not enough for that step[18].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal versions of the first two results. They cover the comparison with the constant 25 × 512⁴, and discrete convexity with 2⁷⁵. The graph-decomposition paper is not in the Lean scope note, so its result remains a claim. No specialist review of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean has checked formal versions of the comparison and discrete-convexity results. The graph decomposition is outside the Lean note, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The probability p at which a random set has a given property half the time.
A list of small sets such that every outcome of the event contains at least one of them.
An assignment of credit to small sets so that every outcome of the event collects total credit at least 1.
The largest p at which some cover has total cost at most one half.
Talagrand's prediction that unions of a few members of a likely family contain almost every set.
A computer program that checks each step of a formally written proof.
